1248-last-of-the-great-scouts-the-life-s:
Helen Cody Wetmore was Buffalo Bill's sister, and she tells her brother's life as she knew it. The tale runs from a Kansas boyhood to work as a Pony Express rider, scouting for the army, and his rise to fame as a buffalo hunter and showman. The book follows Cody from the plains to the Wild West show that toured the world.

Wetmore writes with a sister's pride and a pioneer's memory, mixing family tales with frontier history. The portrait is fond and uncritical, as family memoirs tend to be. The book gives a lively, firsthand-flavored life of the most famous scout of the West.
14604-scandinavian-influence-on-southern:
George Tobias Flom, sometime fellow in German at Columbia, wrote this 1900 study of Scandinavian influence on Southern Lowland Scots, reprinted by AMS Press in 1966. The work treats the linguistic relations of English and Scandinavian.

Flom tests Scots words against Old Norse, Danish, and Swedish forms, rejecting false kinships where sound laws fail. Entries discuss flatlyngis, hap, ledder, and mister, with errata correcting earlier readings. The study is a careful piece of historical linguistics, technical but clear, for readers of Scots and Germanic language history. Flom later taught Scandinavian languages in America.
17262-catalogue-of-linguistic-manuscript:
James C. Pilling's catalogue lists linguistic manuscripts in the library of the Bureau of Ethnology, first printed in the Bureau's First Annual Report for 1879 to 1880. An introductory note traces the set from Henry R. Schoolcraft's work on Native peoples, and the list itself gives manuscript after manuscript on Native tongues, with authors, places, and notes. A table of contents and index were added for this version.

The catalogue is a finding aid, not a narrative: scholars use it to locate papers on languages now rare or lost. Its value lies in scope and order. Linguists and historians of Native America will find a key early guide to the Bureau's holdings on the continent's tongues.
20531-up-to-date-business-including-less:
Up-to-Date Business, published in 1897, is a textbook of commerce for students entering trade and office work. Its lessons include banking and exchange, the machinery by which money moves between firms and countries. The book opens by sorting out its basic terms.

There is a distinction, it says, between the names commerce and business. Commerce is the interchange of products and goods between countries, or between different sections of the same country. Business covers the local work of buying and selling. On those definitions the lessons build, step by step, toward real office practice.
25416-the-abenaki-indians-their-treaties:
Frederic Kidder gathers the early record of the Abenaki people of New England. He prints their treaties of 1713 and 1717 with a historical introduction, and he adds a vocabulary of their language. The book, printed at Portland in 1859, was submitted by request of the Maine Historical Society. Kidder warns that earlier writers tangled the tribal history with rival claims and careless copying.

The vocabulary section reprints extracts from an 1830 Abenaki spelling book called Kimzowi Awighigan. It sets out vowel sounds with English examples, then lists words with translations, such as chols for cricket and kots for goat. Transcriber notes admit some treaty signatures were unclear and were best guessed from the original images.
38859-civil-war-experiences-1862-1865-ch:
Doctor Edward Robbins wrote his civil war experiences from 1862 to 1865, printed at Carthage, Illinois, in November 1919. A portrait fronts the book. Robbins enlisted in Captain John Allen's company on June 7, 1862. Ten days later the company boarded the steamer Jennie Whipple at Dallas City and rode the Mississippi down to Quincy.

At Camp Wood the men were mustered into United States service with nine other companies as the 78th Illinois. His company drew the letter H for its place in line. Battle names head the book, from Chickamauga and Mission Ridge to Atlanta, Jonesboro, and Bentonville. Marches, camps, and fights fill a plain veteran's record, set down in old age.
41103-waterways-of-westward-expansion-th:
Waterways of Westward Expansion, on the Ohio River and its tributaries, is volume nine of Archer Butler Hulbert's Historic Highways of America. It was printed at Cleveland in 1903 with maps. Hulbert opens by saying the Ohio is a greater stream than is generally realized. It drains a vast and rich territory, from latitude forty-two degrees in the north to thirty-seven at its mouth.

Chapters treat the Indian side of the river, the early navigators, the growth of river craft, and three generations of rivermen. Hulbert notes that the Ohio drains more land than the Mississippi above the mouth of the Missouri. Nearly a quarter of the waters that flow into the Gulf of Mexico come from it. Old maps by Bonnecamps, Gordon, and Rufus Putnam picture the river of the pioneers. The book is a history of the waterway that carried settlement west.
42537-the-avifauna-of-micronesia-its-ori:
Rollin Baker wrote a study of the birds of Micronesia, their origin, evolution, and distribution, for the University of Kansas museum series in 1951. The study runs to three hundred fifty nine pages with sixteen figures. It leads a volume that also holds a study of nocturnal bird migration by Lowery and a phylogeny of waxwings by Arvey.

Baker sorts oceanic birds, inshore and offshore kinds, and faunal components of the islands. Migratory shore birds and their original homes get close study. Which birds reached which islands, from where, and how they changed in isolation are his core questions. Museum workers and island naturalists get a full base map of Pacific bird life in this heavy monograph.
46689-burgundy-the-splendid-duchy-storie:
Percy Allen wrote these stories and sketches in south Burgundy. Griffiths printed Burgundy, The Splendid Duchy, in London 1912. Marjorie Nash drew eight water colours and eighty six line drawings. Mont Beuvray fronts the volume as its opening picture plate.

Allen also wrote Impressions of Provence and Songs of Old France. A verse to M on Tant l Vaut of Rochepot opens it. Works consulted list Olivier de la Marche and Comines chronicles. Histories of the Valois dukes of Burgundy stand in the list. Courtépée voyages and a general history of Burgundy stand in the works consulted list.
49966-geology-of-devils-tower-national-m:
Charles Robinson wrote this study of the rock of Devils Tower in Wyoming for the United States Geological Survey. The Park Service and the tower's own history body reprinted it with small changes. A map shows where the monument stands.

Sedimentary rocks fill the first main part: the Spearfish, Gypsum Spring, and Sundance layers. Their parts, from Stockade Beaver shale to Redwater shale, get a page or two each. Stream beds, talus, and landslide stuff follow. Structure and the long past of the rocks lead to the key point: the origin of Devils Tower itself. Plates show its great columns tapering, flaring, and cut by cross cracks.
52625-frank-s-ranche-or-my-holiday-in-th:
An anonymous English sportsman, author of An Amateur Angler's Days in Dovedale and signing himself only E M, wrote this travel book, in its second edition of 1886. Its subtitle calls it a contribution to the inquiry into what we are to do with our boys.

The dedicatory letter thanks his travelling companion for thousands of miles in the great western world, and for always yielding him the best bunk, seat, room, and bed. The introductory note borrows Oliver Wendell Holmes's three reasons for publishing and claims only the third: to tell anything he likes, provided he can make it interesting. He has not been hugged by a bear or scalped, he admits. Holiday readers get a gentleman's Rocky Mountain ranch visit.
60334-a-treatise-on-the-art-of-midwifery:
A Treatise on the Art of Midwifery, by Elizabeth Nihell, attacks instrument practice. Morley printed it at London in 1760, near Beaufort Buildings in the Strand. Nihell wrote as a professed midwife against abuses, above all with instruments. Her question: is it best to employ a man midwife or a midwife.

She addresses the book to all fathers, mothers, and those soon to be either. Common sense can judge the point, she argues, without blind trust in doctors. Interested men may mislead parents, she warns, in this tender concern of families. Nature has not put a fair notion of birth beyond plain reason reach. Her own sense of inequality to the subject opens the plea.
60541-el-ombu:
Hudson wrote this South American tale, first published in 1902 and reissued in the Readers' Library in 1920. Hudson was author of 'Green Mansions,' 'The Purple Land' and 'A Crystal Age' before this book. Spanish verse at the front praises the ombú tree as the glory of the pampa.

Each land has its ruling feature, the verse says, in Hudson's chosen motto. Brazil has its burning sun and Peru its silver mines, the poem runs. Buenos Ayres has its grand pampa, and the pampa has the ombú. Tales of gauchos and plain life gather under that great tree's shade.
8654-the-fallen-star-or-the-history-of-a:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton, writing as E. L. Bulwer, tells the history of a false religion in The Fallen Star, paired here with a dissertation on the origin of evil by Lord Brougham. The publisher's preface, quoting Noah Webster, defines religion as binding anew. Argues that Bulwer shows how easily followers are snared and mentally bound in a labyrinth of falsehood by a designing knave. That impostor builds a new faith and a new priesthood by playing on ignorance and credulity.

Bulwer's point, the preface adds, is general: the history of one supernatural religion. Slight changes, serves to describe them all, since each rests its claim on so-called miracles. Brougham's essay then takes up evil itself, asking where it comes from and how it fits a moral world. Readers get a sceptical Victorian pair, one part story and argument, one part philosophy, both aimed at unmasking priestcraft.
britannica-1911-cebu:
Cebu is a city, port of entry, and capital of Cebu province in the Philippines. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the east coast of Cebu island, north of its centre. Counts from nineteen o three put the city at more than eighteen thousand people.

Wide streets are laid out in a regular plan across the city. A Spanish fort guards the port, which is sheltered from strong winds. Church buildings are praised as very fine in the entry text. The Augustinian church holds a famed image of the Santo Nino. Trade ranks Cebu as the second city of the islands. Hemp, tobacco, sugar, and copra are its chief exports.
britannica-1911-tibbu:
Tibbu, also called Tebu, a nomad people of the eastern Sahara, are the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their name means men of Tu, or of the rocks. Their land touches that of the Tuareg Berbers to the west. The entry puts their domain at some 200,000 square miles.

Their farthest settlements are oases such as Agram, Kawar, and Jebado in the west. Most of the nation is gathered in the region of Tibesti, which gives them their name. Two main groups are named, the northern Teda and the southern Daza. Counts of their numbers range from 60,000 to 100,000, but the entry warns the figures cannot be trusted. The Tibbu are often linked with the Garamantes of Herodotus. Leo Africanus and later writers placed them by turns with Berber or other stocks.
catalogue-of-linguistic-manuscripts-in-t:
James C. Pilling compiled a catalogue of the language manuscripts held by the Bureau of Ethnology, printed in the bureau's first annual report for 1879-80 at Washington. His introduction traces how the stock was gathered. It starts with Henry Schoolcraft's printed form of 350 words, sent to people living among Native tribes. George Gibbs's later forms, used in the Northwest, followed.

The list itself records vocabularies, grammars, and notes language by language, giving each item's size, form, and source. Entries range from a chief's vocabulary taken down in New York in 1863 to word lists from the Colorado River and the Pacific coast. Scholars could see at a glance what the Smithsonian held and what was still missing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cebu:
Cebu is a diocese in the Philippine Islands. It is named for the island on which its city stands, itself named for a fancied resemblance between the island's outline and the Indian ox. Magellan reached Cebu in April 1521. He died in battle on nearby Mactan, leaving behind the Santo Niño statuette, still greatly venerated. The diocese was separated from Manila, which once covered the whole archipelago, on 14 August 1595.

Its territory then covered today's dioceses of Cebu and Jaro, plus the Marian Islands vicariate. It now comprises Cebu, Leyte, Samar, Bohol, Siquijor, Camaguin, and smaller islands nearby. Twenty-two bishops have governed Cebu since its founding, and Thomas Augustine Hendrick, consecrated at Rome in August 1903, became its first American bishop.
doe-osti-2589497-solaero-2020-iii-v-meta:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-5900-96773 closes cooperative project CRD-19-16398 with SolAero Technologies, a maker of space solar cells. Technical contact Ryan France supported work on III-V multi-junction cells, devices that stack several light-absorbing layers to catch more of the spectrum. The hard part is grading between layers whose crystal spacings differ.

Tasks covered design and tuning of those graded buffer layers, doping of materials and junctions, strain-balanced layers, and high-efficiency germanium-based cells. The laboratory advised on test structures the company grew, then helped read the results. In one set, gallium indium arsenide cells with higher doping kept more voltage after radiation exposure, a trait that matters in orbit. Cell voltage loss stayed consistent across alloys tested.
doe-osti-3484930-cybersecurity-risk-prof:
In August 2026, the National Laboratory of the Rockies released report NLR/TP-5T00-86515, which builds cybersecurity risk profiles for systems that manage distributed energy resources. Chelsea Neely, Ryan Cryar, Jennifer Guerra, and Danish Saleem wrote the profiles. Such systems steer rooftop solar, batteries, and flexible loads.

One threat case has a small hacktivist group exploit public firewall details. Loss of visibility during an attack could block voltage control and trip inverters. Utility-scale sites recover faster thanks to stronger defenses and staff. Smaller sites face longer exposure. Profile readers can rank threats by site size and pick defenses that fit.
doe-osti-3682546-improvements-to-radiogr:
Radiography for measuring the buffer layer in TRISO fuel particles is the work of Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4059, dated August 2025. Hannah A. Hutton, Daniel R. Brown, and Grant W. Helmreich are the printed authors. The buffer is a porous carbon coat that takes up gas and shields outer layers from kernel swelling. Its density must be checked against fuel specifications. The old method, mercury porosimetry, cannot judge single particles and makes hazardous waste.

X-ray imaging promises a per-particle check instead. Early trials read buffer density too high, so the team rebuilt the calibration. Grafoil sheets of known density set one curve, and epoxy thickness set another. Two imaging setups with set source and detector distances were compared. Gains were real, yet readings still ran high. Sample preparation limits now stand out as the main block. The report closes with steps to close that gap.
last-of-the-great-scouts-the-life-story-:
Helen Cody Wetmore told the life story of her brother, William F. Cody. The world knew him as Buffalo Bill. She dedicated the book to their mother's memory.

A family genealogy opens the volume, compiled in 1897. It claims descent from Milesius, an old Irish king. The story then follows Cody from boyhood to fame as a scout. Wetmore writes as a sister, with family knowledge and pride. Her book preserves the scout's legend as his own family wished it told. Cody's fame as a showman rests on the scout years told here. Family pride shapes which episodes receive most warmth.
podcast-dannyjones-uQXUNJgtBBU:
Movement coach Ido Portal joins Danny Jones to talk about an ancient tool he says can unlock human power. The episode title quotes his line on the work: it changes you. Portal is a trainer known for fluid, full body movement.

Portal explains his method, which treats the body as one linked system to be trained as a whole. He argues most gym work makes strong parts and a weak whole. Jones asks what proof backs the bold claims. Listeners who train will find a fresh lens on strength and skill. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-n8yZpKsaSbU:
Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor who wrote the Stoic classic Meditations, anchors this Joe Rogan Experience segment. Rogan and his guest look back at Aurelius and other ancient thinkers. The focus is what very old philosophy can still say to people now.

They talk through Stoic habits like facing hardship calmly and focusing on what you can control. The guest explains how Aurelius wrote his notes to himself while running an empire at war. Rogan connects the ideas to training, fighting, and daily stress. It is a plain-spoken intro to Stoic thought through the man who lived it at the top.
podcast-joerogan-qFwiXyZHYbU:
Dr. Robert Malone, a physician and researcher who worked on mRNA technology early in his career, talks with Joe Rogan in episode 2454. Malone became a leading critic of COVID policy and of the vaccines built on that platform. His Rogan visits draw huge audiences and sharp pushback.

Malone lays out his case against the pandemic response, from mandates to how health agencies handled risk data. He explains why he questions the safety reviews behind the shots. Rogan asks how a man from inside the field ended up outside it. The talk captures a central voice of the COVID dissent movement.
scandinavian-influence-on-southern-lowla: George Tobias Flom wrote Scandinavian Influence on Southern Lowland Scotch. Flom was sometime fellow in German at Columbia University. The work studies the links in speech between English and Scandinavian tongues. The printing shown here is a 1966 reprint by AMS Press in New York, with permission of the original publisher, under a copyright of 1900 held by Columbia University Press.
the-fallen-star-or-the-history-of-a-fals:
E. L. Bulwer wrote The Fallen Star, a history of a false religion, and this printing adds a piece on the origin of evil by Lord Brougham. The publisher's preface frames the book as a warning against fraud in faith.

That preface argues that new faiths rise when smooth men play on fear, hope, and love of wonders. It names Joseph Smith and the Mormon faith as a fresh case in a free, schooled land. The tale itself shows a knave founding a creed and a priesthood of his own. Readers are urged to test all claims by plain fact and law.
